candidates.stimulus_use: The operation 'take a common shortcut and qualify it' with the process 'borrowing' suggested the borrowed or shop-bought walking stick that nobody has fitted.
candidates.working_title: A borrowed stick is set to someone else's height
candidates.core_insight: A walking stick helps only when it is the right height, held in the right hand and kept in good repair, and studies of older stick users find these basics are often wrong.
candidates.angle: Picking up a stick from the chemist or a relative's cupboard is a common shortcut; three checks that anyone can do at home turn it into a safer aid.
candidates.position: Anyone who uses a walking stick should have its height, the hand it is held in and the rubber tip checked, ideally by a physiotherapist, rather than assuming any stick will do.
claims_needing_evidence: The top of a stick should be level with the crease of the wrist when the person stands upright with arms relaxed at the sides (clinical review: Bradley and Hernandez 2011)
A stick is normally held in the hand opposite the weak or painful leg and moved forward at the same time as that leg (clinical review: Bradley and Hernandez 2011)

Among older people who use sticks, incorrect height, poor maintenance, use in the wrong hand and lack of professional advice when choosing the stick are common (cross-sectional study: Liu HH et al. 2010)
A worn rubber tip (ferrule) grips less well and should be replaced (NHS or physiotherapy patient information; source to find)

candidates.pause: Many households have a spare stick in a cupboard and have never thought about its height.

candidates.follow: Specific, practical advice that respects the person's independence.

candidates.stimulus_use: The same shortcut operation, with the GP viewpoint and the timescale 'a year', pointed to the everyday advice 'take it easy' after an illness at home and what follows over the next months.
candidates.working_title: 'Take it easy' needs an end date
candidates.core_insight: Episodes of staying in bed or cutting down usual activities because of illness at home, not only hospital stays, are linked with later loss of independence, so rest after an illness should have a planned end.
candidates.angle: Deconditioning is usually discussed as a hospital problem; a monthly-interview cohort found restricted activity at home predicted functional decline in people who were otherwise at low or intermediate risk, and the link was absent in people already at high risk.
candidates.position: After an illness at home, advice to rest should come with a plan and a date for getting back to usual activity.
claims_needing_evidence: In a cohort of 680 community-living people aged 70 and over, each additional month with restricted activity (at least half a day in bed or cutting down usual activities because of illness, injury or another problem) was associated with a worse disability score at 18 months after adjustment (cohort study: Gill, Allore and Guo 2003)
The association was present in people at low and intermediate baseline risk of disability and not statistically significant in the high-risk group (Gill 2003)
The finding is an association and does not show that rest itself causes decline (Gill 2003 design)
Hospital stays and restricted activity at home are both linked with the onset of new disability (cohort study: Gill et al. 2004 JAMA; to verify)

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation 'apply it to the poorest or most isolated person' and the word 'tailoring' led to strength and balance training fitted into a person's own daily routine instead of a class they must travel to.
candidates.working_title: Strength and balance training without a class
candidates.core_insight: Strength and balance exercises built into daily routines at home, taught by a therapist, reduced falls and improved strength and function in a randomised trial, which makes them an option for people unable to get to a class.
candidates.angle: Advice to join a strength and balance class assumes transport, money and confidence; the LiFE approach brings the training to the person's own chair, worktop and stairs, but it still needs a therapist to teach it.
candidates.position: People who are housebound, isolated or unable to attend classes should be offered home-based strength and balance training; LiFE is one tested way to do it (judgement, supported by the trial).
claims_needing_evidence: In the LiFE trial (317 people aged 70 and over with recent falls, Sydney), the lifestyle-integrated programme reduced the rate of falls by about 31% compared with a gentle-exercise control (1.66 versus 2.28 falls per person-year) (RCT: Clemson et al. 2012 BMJ)
The LiFE group had better static balance, ankle strength, function and participation than controls (Clemson 2012)
LiFE was taught at home over five sessions with two booster visits and two phone calls (Clemson 2012)
LiFE activities include specific everyday strength and balance moves such as sit-to-stand and standing heel to toe (LiFE manual; examples to verify)
The trial excluded people with moderate to severe cognitive problems, people unable to walk independently and care home residents (Clemson 2012)
Transport, cost and confidence are reported barriers to older people taking part in exercise classes (qualitative systematic review; to verify)

candidates.angle: The moment of leaving home is the easiest chance to bring the equipment that lets the person keep walking on the ward, and it is easily missed in an emergency.
candidates.position: The person's own walking aid, well-fitting shoes and glasses should reach the ward as early as practical.

candidates.stimulus_use: The bus pass and 'waiting' prompted the walk to the shop or bus, and the operation 'ask who bears the cost' pointed to who pays when crossing times assume a faster walker.
candidates.working_title: Crossings timed for a speed most older people do not walk
candidates.core_insight: UK pedestrian crossing timings have assumed a walking speed of 1.2 metres per second, and a national survey found that most people over 65 in England walked more slowly than that.
candidates.angle: Walking speed is usually treated as a clinical measure; the same number decides whether an older person can cross to the shop or the bus stop before the lights change, and it links to who goes out at all.
candidates.position: An older person's ability to get out depends on streets as well as legs; crossing times set above most older people's walking speed shift the cost onto older pedestrians. The post reports the study authors' own recommendation to revise timings as theirs and proposes no specific policy.
claims_needing_evidence: UK pedestrian crossings assume a walking speed of 1.2 m/s (Asher et al. 2012; confirm against current Department for Transport guidance)

In Health Survey for England 2005 data on 3,145 adults aged 65 and over, mean walking speed was 0.9 m/s in men and 0.8 m/s in women, and 84% of men and 93% of women walked slower than 1.2 m/s or could not do the test (cross-sectional study: Asher 2012)
Female sex, older age, lower socioeconomic status, poorer health and lower grip strength were associated with walking impairment (Asher 2012)
The study authors recommended that crossing timings be reconsidered (Asher 2012)

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation 'change the scale (one person to a population, or the reverse)' with the quality 'drift' led to the difference between a population predictor and one person's slowing walk.
candidates.working_title: Gait speed: a population predictor used on one person
candidates.core_insight: Usual walking speed predicts survival across large groups of older people, but for an individual it is most useful as a prompt to look for treatable causes of slowness and as a measure to repeat, not as a personal prognosis.
candidates.angle: The same measurement means different things at population and individual scale; the useful clinical move is serial measurement and a search for reasons.
candidates.position: Measure and repeat usual gait speed in older patients; treat a slow or slowing result as a reason for assessment, and avoid presenting it to a person as their life expectancy.
claims_needing_evidence: In a pooled analysis of 9 cohorts (34,485 community-dwelling adults aged 65 and over), faster gait speed was associated with longer survival, pooled hazard ratio 0.88 per 0.1 m/s (Studenski et al. 2011 JAMA)
At age 75, predicted 10-year survival across the range of gait speeds ranged from 19% to 87% in men and from 35% to 91% in women (Studenski 2011)
Prediction from age, sex and gait speed was as accurate as prediction using chronic conditions, smoking, blood pressure, body mass index and hospitalisation (Studenski 2011)
The cohorts were collected between 1986 and 2000 and were about 80% white, which limits generalisation (Studenski 2011)
A gait speed of 0.8 m/s or less indicates poor physical performance in the European sarcopenia definition (Cruz-Jentoft et al. 2019)
Common causes of slow gait include joint pain, parkinsonism, neuropathy, heart and lung disease, low mood and medicines (clinical review; source to find)

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation 'compare the stated aim of a service with what happens' and the word 'averages' pointed to reablement's aim of restoring independence set against a headline measure that records only where the person lives.

candidates.angle: The stated aim of reablement is independence and the person's own goals; the headline measure is location.

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation 'change the viewpoint to someone else in the scene' with the physiotherapist viewpoint and the word 'distance' led to the therapist asked to certify safety at a distance from the person's actual home and choices.
candidates.working_title: 'Is she safe for discharge?'
candidates.core_insight: Asking a therapist whether someone is 'safe for discharge' asks for a certainty that no assessment gives; a better record states what the person can do, what could go wrong, what reduces the risk and what the person wants.
candidates.angle: Seen from the physiotherapist's side, the word 'safe' shifts responsibility and hides a decision that belongs largely to the person, with support.
candidates.position: Replace 'safe for discharge' with a stated account of abilities, risks, mitigations and the person's view; a person with capacity may accept risks that others would not (judgement grounded in capacity law).

candidates.position: Discharge planning should check the specific tasks of arriving home, and families are entitled to ask about each one.

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation 'examine a neglected consequence' with the word 'margins' led to the small margin of strength that weaker people have for everyday tasks, and what happens when it shrinks or grows.
candidates.working_title: Why small strength changes affect the weakest most

candidates.working_title: Ask when she last walked

candidates.working_title: Sarcopenia is found by weakness first
candidates.core_insight: Under the 2019 European definition, low muscle strength measured by grip or chair-rise time identifies probable sarcopenia and is enough in clinical practice to look for causes and start treatment, with muscle quantity measured to confirm.

candidates.working_title: What prehabilitation trials in frail older people found
candidates.core_insight: Exercise and nutrition before surgery (prehabilitation) is plausible and widely promoted, but a randomised trial in frail older people having bowel cancer surgery found no fewer complications, and overall evidence certainty is low.
candidates.angle: An intervention whose benefits are often overstated; the gap between a sound rationale and trial results changes how to counsel patients.
candidates.position: Prehabilitation can be offered for its possible benefits, but frail older patients should not be told it will reduce their complications.
claims_needing_evidence: In an RCT of 110 frail patients aged 65 and over (mean 78) having colorectal cancer resection within an enhanced recovery pathway, multimodal prehabilitation did not reduce 30-day complications compared with the same programme started after surgery (RCT: Carli et al. 2020)
Secondary outcomes, including recovery of walking capacity, did not differ between groups (Carli 2020)
The programme length before surgery was about 4 weeks (Carli 2020; to verify)

An umbrella review found low to very low certainty evidence that exercise prehabilitation reduces complications, non-home discharge and length of stay, and moderate certainty evidence of improved functional recovery in cancer surgery (umbrella review: McIsaac et al. 2022)

candidates.working_title: Parkinson's medicines on time keep people moving
candidates.core_insight: In hospital, people with Parkinson's who receive their medicines late, missed or wrong are more likely to leave with worse movement, and letting people take their own medicines where safe is one protection.
candidates.angle: Medicine timing in Parkinson's is a mobility issue; a standard drug-round schedule can undo a person's carefully timed regime.
candidates.position: People with Parkinson's in hospital should get their medicines at their usual times, including by self-administration where safe, and families should ask for this on admission.
claims_needing_evidence: In a survey of 684 people with Parkinson's in the Netherlands, among those admitted in the previous year 21% reported motor deterioration and 26% received incorrect anti-Parkinson medication; incorrect medication was associated with deterioration (survey: Gerlach et al. 2012)

NICE guidance recommends that people with Parkinson's in hospital or care homes can take their medicines at the right times, including self-administration where appropriate (NICE NG71 2017; wording to verify)

candidates.working_title: Up, dressed and moving: reading the evidence

candidates.angle: A popular campaign deserves the same reading as any intervention: the problem is well evidenced, the campaign's own effect is less certain, and doing it consistently is the hard part.
candidates.position: Keep the aims of End PJ paralysis, and measure whether patients are actually up, dressed and walking rather than assuming the campaign has changed practice.

candidates.working_title: Protein drinks work best alongside strength exercise
candidates.core_insight: Nutritional supplements taken without exercise did not improve strength in a care home trial, and guidelines recommend resistance exercise as the main treatment for age-related muscle loss, with protein as a support.
candidates.angle: Families often buy protein drinks hoping to rebuild strength; the evidence points to putting the effort into strength exercise and enough protein at meals, while people who are losing weight need assessment and nutritional support in their own right.
candidates.position: For muscle weakness in older age, resistance exercise is the first treatment; protein helps alongside it, and a supplement alone is unlikely to restore strength.
claims_needing_evidence: In a trial in 100 frail nursing home residents, a multinutrient supplement had no effect on any primary outcome, while resistance training increased strength and gait speed (RCT: Fiatarone et al. 1994)
International sarcopenia guidelines strongly recommend resistance-based physical activity and conditionally recommend protein supplementation or a protein-rich diet (guideline: Dent et al. 2018)
Expert groups recommend protein intakes of about 1.0 to 1.2 g per kg of body weight per day for healthy older adults (PROT-AGE: Bauer et al. 2013; ESPEN: Deutz et al. 2014; to verify)
Adding protein supplementation to resistance training gives modest additional gains in muscle mass or strength (meta-analysis, e.g. Liao et al. 2017; to verify)
People who are malnourished or losing weight should be assessed and offered nutrition support (NICE CG32)
